text: In the past. <break time="0.8s" /> It was often assumed. <break time="0.8s" /> That competence acquired in the first language L1. <break time="0.8s" /> Was qualitatively different. <break time="0.8s" /> From that in a second language L2. <break time="0.8s" /> Or any subsequent language. <break time="0.8s" /> This privileging of the native language. <break time="0.8s" /> Led to many popular misconceptions. <break time="0.8s" /> Such as believing. <break time="0.8s" /> That children of bilingual parents. <break time="0.8s" /> Would never fully acquire either language. <break time="0.8s" /> Remaining somehow linguistically disadvantaged. <break time="0.8s" /> Such claims are due to the belief. <break time="0.8s" /> That monolingualism is the norm. <break time="0.8s" /> And they are held by many. <break time="0.8s" /> In the United States and other countries. <break time="0.8s" /> Where a single language is politically or socially dominant. <break time="0.8s" /> That this view must be wrong. <break time="0.8s" /> Can easily be seen from the fact. <break time="0.8s" /> That many people in the world. <break time="0.8s" /> Are speaking more than one language. <break time="0.8s" /> In fact it is bilingualism or trilingualism. <break time="0.8s" /> Rather than monolingualism. <break time="0.8s" /> That is most common. <break time="0.8s" /> Even in supposedly monolingual nations. <break time="0.8s" /> Like the United States. <break time="0.8s" /> US Census figures from 2014 showed. <break time="0.8s" /> That at least 20 percent of the population. <break time="0.8s" /> Regularly spoke a language other than English. <break time="0.8s" /> And 53 percent of these people. <break time="0.8s" /> Also spoke English.
